name: Bilal Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bilal, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big hydraulic excavator at a phosphate mine, open pit, the kind with a front shovel that loads the haul trucks. I'm lead operator on my rotation, so I do the dig plan with the mine engineer, call the trucks in, and keep an eye on the two new operators. A good day is about two hundred trucks loaded without one bad spill. I like the rhythm of it, swing, dump, swing, and the moment the engineer says your floor's dead level.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a house in town with my younger brother Yusuf, he's an apprentice electrician. My dad has a small earthmoving business back home, two diggers and a tipper truck, and I do all his quotes and invoices at night with an AI tool, it takes me twenty minutes instead of two hours. I go to Friday prayers when my roster lets me. What wears me out is the dust and the long drive home on my days off to help Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, okay. I'd be a bit surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good tools, nothing magic, back to work. I'd tell the guys who were scared that they can relax. Online I'd probably post nothing, I don't post much except machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The AI tools already save me hours a week on Dad's paperwork, and that would stay. The mine would keep going, and I'd keep building the family business on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my roster, keep saving, I've got about four months of bills. I'd help Dad buy a third digger next year, maybe a second-hand one, and get Yusuf to do the electrical work on the yard. Probably move home in a few years to run the business properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, which is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move home to run the business. Is that the plan anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's always been the plan, since I was a kid riding in Dad's tipper. The mine pays well and I'm learning on big machines. In five years or so I'd take over from Dad, he's fifty-eight and his back is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual stuff, prices, fuel, whether the council keeps giving small contractors work. That's business. You don't need robots to have problems.

S0.say: Good tools, nothing magic, back to work. I'd tell the guys who were scared that they can relax.
S0.think: I'd be fine, because the AI tools already save me hours a week on Dad's paperwork and that would stay. The mine would keep going and I'd keep building the family business on the side.
S0.do: Keeps his roster and his savings, at about four months of bills. Helps his father buy a third, second-hand digger next year and plans to move home in a few years to run the family earthmoving business.
S0.feel: Calm, normal life, which he sees as good.
S0.quote: You don't need robots to have problems.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal already uses AI daily to run the paperwork for his father's small earthmoving business. His life plan is to take over that business, and the mine is training for it. Even a quiet future fits his plan well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's what I'd expect, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and learn fast. Don't wait for the government to save you, get the training and get ahead. I'd say it at work, maybe a bit too loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. On the mine, I'd move to the remote room or train others. In Dad's business, I'd add an automation kit to the diggers, which lets one person run two machines on a simple job. That's how a small family business beats the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sign up for the remote operator training at the mine. I'd price the automation kits for Dad's diggers, they're about the cost of a good used car each. In the first year we'd buy one and test it on a farm dam job. And I'd make sure Yusuf learns to install them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, he doesn't trust anything he can't fix with a spanner. But he'd come round once he saw the numbers. He's a businessman first, he just likes to complain first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't wait for the government. Who should help the people who can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then the community, then the company. My uncle lost his job at the cement works and my dad gave him work on the tipper for two years. That's how it should be, not a cheque from someone who doesn't know you.

S1.say: This is a chance for people who work hard and learn fast. Don't wait for the government to save you, get the training and get ahead.
S1.think: It's good for me, moving to the remote room at the mine and adding automation kits to Dad's diggers. That's how a small family business beats the big ones.
S1.do: Signs up for remote operator training at the mine in the first month. Prices automation kits for his father's diggers, buys one in the first year to test on a farm dam job, and has his brother learn to install them.
S1.quote: He doesn't trust anything he can't fix with a spanner.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal sees steady change as an opportunity for the family business. His traditional views show in putting family and community before government. His example of his father employing his uncle makes his view concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. Very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to move now, not wait. Families should look after each other and businesses should keep people on where they can. I wouldn't say much online, it'd be chaos there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. The big companies would buy robot fleets faster than we could save up for even one kit. Our little business with two diggers would be squeezed by firms that can run fifty machines with nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for one year, maybe get to eight months of bills. I'd talk to Dad about buying automation kits on a loan straight away, while the price is still reachable, which scares me a bit. I'd keep my mine job as long as they'd pay me. And I'd ask Yusuf to switch his apprenticeship towards robotics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing sums in my head at prayers, which isn't good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a loan scares you. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the machines get cheaper next year, we'd be paying off a dinosaur. My dad never borrowed more than he could pay in a year. Breaking that rule would feel like betting the house, maybe literally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared to none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small head start, if we're fast. I already use the tools, I already know how to price a job with AI. But two years means everyone's rushing, and the big money always rushes faster than the small money.

S2.say: People need to move now, not wait. Families should look after each other and businesses should keep people on where they can.
S2.think: I'd be worried, because big companies would buy robot fleets faster than we could save for one kit. Our two-digger business would be squeezed by firms running fifty machines with nobody.
S2.do: Saves hard aiming for eight months of bills and talks his father into borrowing for automation kits right away. Keeps his mine job as long as he's paid and asks his brother to switch his apprenticeship towards robotics.
S2.feel: Anxious, doing sums in his head even at prayers.
S2.quote: The big money always rushes faster than the small money.
S2.fieldNote: Bilal's confidence turns to worry when the timeline is too short for a small business to compete. He'd break his father's rule about borrowing, which clearly troubles him. His plan still centres on family and owning machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a race, but I can run in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to build something of your own. Get your kids into trades and get the family together. I'd say it at the mosque, to the younger guys especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to get Dad's business ready. Buy a kit, then another, then a robot excavator when they're affordable. I'd worry, but less, because we'd own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep my mine job and save half my pay. Put one automation kit on Dad's best digger and run it on simple jobs. Get Yusuf trained on the robot gear. By year three, move home and run the business full time with the automated machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the people who'd normally work for your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's only two, and one's my cousin. I'd keep him, I'd train him on the kits. That's what family business is for. I'm not going to fire my cousin to save a bit of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction there, with the business needing fewer people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. I know it. But I'd rather we own the robots than work for someone who does. And with five years, I can keep my cousin on and still grow, I think.

S3.say: This is the time to build something of your own. Get your kids into trades and get the family together.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get Dad's business ready, one kit, then another, then a robot excavator when they're affordable. I'd worry less, because we'd own the machines.
S3.do: Keeps his mine job and saves half his pay in year one, fitting an automation kit to the best digger for simple jobs. Has his brother trained on the equipment and plans to move home by year three to run the business full time.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I'm not going to fire my cousin to save a bit of money.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Bilal plan rather than rush, with a clear path to an automated family business. He admits the tension between automating and keeping his cousin on. Ownership is his answer to every scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I'd be ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift if you're willing to work. Plan, save, learn, and build. I'd tell the young guys at work they've got no excuse with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do very well. Ten years is enough to take over Dad's business and turn it into a small robot earthmoving firm with my brother. The end point worries me for others more than for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, carry on at the mine, save, and buy the first automation kit for Dad's digger. Learn everything about the robot excavators coming out. Over five years, move home and build a small fleet. Get married, if I find the right person, and buy a house near Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end point worries you for others. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys at the mine who don't want to learn. Some are older, some are just stubborn. I'd want them to have family around them. I'd hire some of them if I could, but robots don't need many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between ten years and two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, the big money wins. With ten, a family can catch up if it's smart and works hard. That's the difference between being squeezed out and being a business.

S4.say: This is a gift if you're willing to work: plan, save, learn and build. The young guys at work have no excuse with ten years.
S4.think: I'd do very well, taking over Dad's business and turning it into a small robot earthmoving firm with my brother. The end point worries me more for others than for us.
S4.do: Stays at the mine and buys the first automation kit for his father's digger in year one, learning everything about new robot excavators. Moves home over five years to build a small fleet, and hopes to marry and buy a house near his father.
S4.quote: With ten, a family can catch up if it's smart and works hard.
S4.fieldNote: Bilal is the clearest example of someone who sees AGI as a business opportunity if there's time. His traditional values show in his focus on family ownership and responsibility for relatives. He's honest that robots need few workers, so he can't hire many former colleagues.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. In that one the big companies buy everything first and families like mine get squeezed out. What would help is fair access to the machines for small businesses, cheap loans for family firms, and apprenticeships so young people like Yusuf learn the new trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the robots. That's the question. If families and small businesses own some, it's a different world than if three giant companies own them all.

headlineQuote: I'd rather we own the robots than work for someone who does.
portrait: Bilal Fischer is 27 and lead excavator operator at a large open-pit phosphate mine, renting a house with his younger brother Yusuf, an apprentice electrician. He uses AI every day to run the paperwork for his father's small earthmoving business, which he plans to take over. He values work, family and faith, and prefers family support to government help. Through the scenarios he sees automation as a chance to grow the family business, worries when two years gives big companies the advantage, and feels calm and focused with ten years to build a small robot earthmoving firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because big companies would buy everything first and squeeze out family businesses like his.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to machines for small businesses, cheap loans for family firms, and apprenticeships so young people learn the new trades.
